page-privacy-public-by-default-wallet-ac: Many people keep a few accounts: one for savings, one for trading, one for trying new apps. The wallet shows them all on one screen, so it asks for every balance at once. The server sees one IP address ask about all of them in the same second. To that server, your “separate” accounts were never separate.

The price lookup works the same way. To show your portfolio in your currency, the wallet sends a price service the exact list of tokens you hold, from the same IP address. That's a sketch of your finances, shared with a service you may never have heard of.
page-privacy-public-by-default-wallet-ht: The technical bit: doesn't HTTPS protect this?

HTTPS encrypts the request on its way through the café Wi-Fi and your internet provider. The server at the other end still has to read your request to answer it. It sees a request like {request} in plain text, next to your IP address and the time.

Some wallets send these requests through their own servers first, so the <glossary>RPC</glossary> provider (the service that answers your wallet's questions about the blockchain) and the price service don't see your IP address. That helps, but now you're trusting the wallet company's logs instead.
page-privacy-public-by-default-wallet-nf: The gift you didn't ask for

Anyone can send you an NFT, and you can't refuse it. The picture usually lives off the blockchain, often on a server the sender controls. When your wallet or a marketplace shows it, your device fetches the picture, which tells that server your IP address and exactly when you looked.

A sender who mints a different token for each target can tell from the image address alone which wallet is looking. It works like the tracking pixel in a marketing email, except you can't unsubscribe.

This only works when your wallet fetches the image straight from the sender's server. Many wallets load NFT images through their own proxy or from a cache, so the sender sees the wallet company's server, not you.

page-privacy-public-by-default-wallet-di: Every website can see your wallets

Browser wallets announce themselves to every page you open. That's how a Connect button knows which wallets to offer. It also means any site can list your installed wallets without asking, before you click anything. This page can do it too, but it only counts them. Try it.

No wallet answered. There may be no browser wallet installed here, or yours may not support this kind of announcement yet. On an ordinary website, an installed wallet that supports it answers straight away.
This page only counts the wallets that answer, using a standard called EIP-6963. It doesn't show or keep their names, never connects, never asks for your addresses and sends nothing anywhere.

Combine that with the browser fingerprint from the first chapter, and trackers can recognize “the person with these two wallets on this laptop in this time zone” from site to site. page-privacy-public-by-default-rpc-title: The service you ask about everything
page-privacy-public-by-default-rpc-nav-b: The service your wallet asks about everything. Your wallet probably chose it for you.
page-privacy-public-by-default-rpc-lede: Your wallet doesn't read the blockchain itself. It asks a provider's server, which sees your balances, the names you look up and every transaction you send, a moment before anyone else does.
page-privacy-public-by-default-rpc-intro: Ethereum runs on thousands of computers called <glossary>nodes</glossary>. Each keeps its own copy of the chain and answers questions about it: what's the balance of this address, and did this transaction land? Running a node takes a couple of terabytes of fast storage and a machine that stays on, so most wallets don't run one. They send their questions to someone else's node through a standard interface called RPC (remote procedure call).
The service that runs that node is your <glossary>RPC</glossary> provider. The wallet maker usually picks it for you, and everything your wallet shows you comes from asking it.
page-privacy-public-by-default-rpc-quote: “The node provider can see the user's IP address, device fingerprint, specific queried addresses, and the timing and frequency of their activity.”
From <link>the privacy roadmap for Ethereum</link> on ethereum.org
page-privacy-public-by-default-rpc-view-: This is what a provider could piece together from an ordinary week, and the customer is you. Switch the setup to see what each change hides and what still gets through.
The RPC provider's view of you
Your wallet's default setup. One provider sees your IP address, every address you ask about, when you ask, and every transaction you send.

Tor hides your IP address, but the wallet still asks about all your accounts in the same session, seconds apart. The provider can't see who you are. It can still see that those accounts belong to one person.

Each account gets its own Tor connection, so the provider sees several unrelated customers. They all show up within a few minutes of each other every morning, though, and that timing can tie them back together.

Your wallet asks a node you run, so there's no provider to see anything. Your transactions still have to go out to the network, and your node's peers can see where they came from. That's the next chapter.

Look at the log again. Before you paid {friend}, your wallet asked the provider to look up that name, because <glossary>ENS</glossary> names like it are stored on the chain. So the provider knew who you were about to pay. Then the payment itself went through the same provider, which saw the signed transaction before the rest of the network did.
page-privacy-public-by-default-rpc-logs-: Some providers say they keep no logs, and some public lists of RPC endpoints label which ones say they don't track you.

That label only repeats what the provider says, and nobody outside the company can check it. Policies change, servers get breached, and a company can be ordered to hand over what it has. A policy also does nothing about people watching the traffic on its way there.
page-privacy-public-by-default-rpc-recor: Someone who can watch internet traffic, such as an internet service provider, can see when a wallet keeps asking an RPC service whether a transaction has landed. Matching that timing to when the transaction appears on chain linked IP addresses to blockchain addresses more than 95% of the time, against ordinary users on Ethereum, Bitcoin and Solana. The researchers didn't need to break any encryption.
Source: Wang et al., <link>“Time Tells All: Deanonymization of Blockchain RPC Users with Zero Transaction Fee”</link>, ACM CCS 2025
page-privacy-public-by-default-rpc-home-: The obvious fix is to run your own node, so there's no provider to watch you. Plenty of people have done the hard part and have a fully synced node running at home.

Their wallets often still use the default provider, because a phone can't reach the node from outside the house without extra setup. So every balance check still goes to the provider, and the node at home does nothing for their privacy.
Where your phone's questions actually go
Your phone can't reach your node at home, so it asks the default RPC provider instead.
A VPN to your own node closes the gap. Some <link>home node setups</link> include one.
page-privacy-public-by-default-rpc-priva: Ethereum researchers split the problem into three parts. A wallet needs all three to read the chain privately and still trust the answers.
The provider sees someone else's IP address instead of yours. Tor and mixnets do this, if your wallet lets you use them. Some providers block Tor traffic, so not every service will answer.
<link>Learn about Tor and other ways to hide your IP address</link>
The server answers without learning which address you asked about. The technique is called private information retrieval, or PIR.
A <glossary>light client</glossary> checks the provider's answers against the chain, so the provider can't lie to you.
Don't mistake the third part for the first two. A light client still asks the provider about your addresses. A light client protects you from being lied to. It doesn't stop you from being watched.
page-privacy-public-by-default-rpc-pir-s: The technical bit: how can a server answer without knowing the question?
page-privacy-public-by-default-rpc-pir-1: The simplest version is to download the whole database and look up the answer yourself. The server learns nothing, but the database is very large.
page-privacy-public-by-default-rpc-pir-2: PIR schemes use encryption instead. You send an encrypted query, the server runs it over its whole database without being able to read it, and you get back an encrypted answer only you can open. That costs the server far more work per question, which is why it isn't in wallets yet. Infrastructure teams are testing implementations now.
page-privacy-public-by-default-rpc-fixno: The strongest option is a wallet that uses your own node, from every device you use. Without one, hiding your IP address and giving each account its own connection, at different times, makes your accounts harder to link. Treat “no logs” as a claim you can't check. <link>Learn about running a node</link>.
page-privacy-public-by-default-network-n: How a pending transaction spreads, who listens to it, and what bots can do before it lands.
page-privacy-public-by-default-network-l: The moment you send it, your transaction passes from computer to computer until thousands of them hold a copy they can read before it's final. A few of those computers only listen, and note where each transaction came from.
page-privacy-public-by-default-network-i: No central server receives your transaction. Your wallet or RPC provider hands it to a <glossary>node</glossary>, which passes it to the nodes it's connected to, called its peers. They pass it to theirs.
Within seconds it sits in <glossary>mempools</glossary> around the world. A mempool is a node's waiting room for transactions that aren't in a block yet.
That's part of what keeps Ethereum open. Anyone can run a node and see what's waiting to happen, or run one that only listens.
page-privacy-public-by-default-network-h: A listening node connects to as many peers as it can and notes when each new transaction arrives and which peer delivered it. The first peer to deliver it is often the one closest to where it started. Put a few listeners on the network, compare notes, and the origin stands out.

page-privacy-public-by-default-network-o: This works even if you run your own node. Your node has to tell its peers about your transaction, and they know its IP address. A listener connected to thousands of nodes is likely to be one of them. Running a node hides what you read. It doesn't hide where your transactions start.
page-privacy-public-by-default-network-r: The same kind of listening works on Ethereum's network. Researchers ran four nodes for three days and, from what they collected, located more than 15% of Ethereum's validators, linking them to the IP addresses of the machines running them. Validators are the participants that propose and vote on blocks.
Source: Heimbach, Vonlanthen, Villacis, Kiffer and Wattenhofer, “Deanonymizing Ethereum Validators: The P2P Network Has a Privacy Issue”, USENIX Security 2025
page-privacy-public-by-default-network-q: “Network-level privacy is the Achilles heel of financial privacy in cryptocurrencies.”
Béres, Seres, Kelen and Benczúr, “ethp2psim: Evaluating and deploying privacy-enhanced peer-to-peer routing protocols for the Ethereum network”, arXiv preprint, 2023
page-privacy-public-by-default-network-m: The mempool shows your next move
While your transaction waits for a block, anyone can read it. For a payment to a friend, that's a privacy problem. For a trade, it can also cost you money.
page-privacy-public-by-default-network-r: One widely tracked sandwich bot ran about 238,000 sandwich attacks on more than 106,000 victims in roughly three months, according to figures from an MEV analytics firm.
page-privacy-public-by-default-network-p: You can skip the public mempool. Some RPC endpoints send your transaction straight to <glossary>block builders</glossary>, the services that put blocks together, instead of passing it around the network. This is a private transaction channel, sometimes called an MEV-protected RPC.
Privacy tools often use relayers, which submit a transaction for you so it doesn't come from your address or your IP address.

Both hide your trade from bots and your origin from listeners, but they put one service between you and the network. That service sees your transaction and, unless you connect over Tor, your IP address. Many say they don't keep logs. As with RPC providers, you can't check that from outside.

Some private channels also share hints about your pending transaction with searchers, the bots that look for <glossary>MEV</glossary>, usually in return for paying you back part of the value. What a channel shares, and with whom, is worth checking before you rely on it.
page-privacy-public-by-default-network-c: A relay or builder can also refuse a transaction, and a transaction that never lands protects nobody. Ethereum's <link>privacy roadmap</link> notes that large block builders can quietly leave out transactions from privacy tools.

A planned change called FOCIL (EIP-7805) would let a committee of validators list the valid transactions they've seen, and have blocks that leave those transactions out rejected. It is scheduled for the Hegotá upgrade.

The roadmap pairs this with what it calls compliance-aware privacy: designs where people can prove their funds aren't connected to known malicious addresses without revealing the rest of their activity, so private transactions can also meet regulatory requirements.
page-privacy-public-by-default-network-f: The deeper fix is a network that hides where a transaction started. A node could pass a new transaction along a random path before it spreads, or wrap it in layers of encryption the way Tor does, so a listener couldn't easily tell who sent it.

Another blockchain, Monero, adopted a design like this, called <link>Dandelion++</link>, in 2020. Ethereum's network doesn't work this way today, and every privacy tool built on Ethereum still has to cross it.
How this can be fixed · Part II

A private transaction channel keeps bots from seeing a trade before it lands, in exchange for trusting the channel. Sending transactions to an RPC endpoint over Tor hides your IP address from the service that receives them. Any relay can still refuse a transaction, which is why inclusion rules like FOCIL matter.

page-privacy-public-by-default-chain-ind: Public for as long as the chain exists
Everything in this chapter works with today's tools. The data doesn't expire, and matching patterns across millions of transactions keeps getting cheaper as analysis tools improve.

Some privacy designs rely on encryption that a large enough quantum computer could break one day. If that happens, it could reveal who paid whom, years after the fact. Anyone can save a copy of today's chain and wait. Security researchers call this "harvest now, decrypt later."
page-privacy-public-by-default-chain-pul: On a public ledger, your privacy has to hold up against tools that haven't been built yet.
page-privacy-public-by-default-chain-tec: The technical bit: what's in a transaction, and can old history disappear?

A transaction carries your address, the recipient, the amount, the data for any contract call, your fee settings, a counter called the <glossary>nonce</glossary>, and your signature. The block adds a timestamp. All of it is public.

Since mid-2025, Ethereum nodes may delete block history from before the Merge to save disk space. This is called <link>partial history expiry</link>. It doesn't make anything private: full copies stay available from public archives and block explorers.
page-privacy-public-by-default-chain-fix: You can't delete what's already public, but you can add less to it. Separate addresses for separate parts of your life, <glossary>stealth addresses</glossary> for receiving payments, shielded pools for savings, and an address book instead of copying from your history each reduce what a single payment reveals. Part II covers each one, with its trade-offs.
page-privacy-public-by-default-chain-nex: The firms that connect addresses to people, and why they exist.
page-privacy-public-by-default-analysts-: Witness {number} · The analysts
Seven wallets, one person
The companies whose job is connecting addresses to each other.
You did the careful thing and gave each purpose its own wallet. To an analyst they can still look like one cluster. Joining them up is the job.

Reading the ledger is an industry. Chain-analysis companies such as Chainalysis, TRM Labs and Elliptic sell software that groups addresses into entities and labels them. Their customers include exchanges, banks and government agencies.
The industry exists because those customers need it: exchanges use it to meet anti-money-laundering rules, and investigators use it to trace stolen funds after hacks and scams.
Some analytics platforms show their labels to anyone who searches, and block explorers add name tags too.

Their main tool is the heuristic, a rule of thumb that ties two addresses to the same owner. The ones below need nothing but the public chain. Apply them one at a time to seven addresses that look unrelated.
The fresh-wallet trap

A new address can't do anything until it holds ETH to pay <glossary>gas</glossary>. Fund it from your main wallet and it isn't fresh anymore. Fund it from an exchange instead and it's tied to your exchange account, which has your name on it. This is one of the hardest links to avoid, because a clean way around it isn't built into Ethereum yet.
Part II covers the options people use today. <link>Frame transactions (EIP-8141)</link>, scheduled for the Hegotá upgrade, would let another account pay the gas, so a fresh address could stay fresh.

A researcher at TU Berlin tested three heuristics on Ethereum's first four years: reuse of the same exchange deposit address, collecting airdrops from several sign-ups into one address, and token approvals between one's own addresses. Together they grouped 17.9% of all active user accounts into clusters, pointing to more than 340,000 people or organizations that each ran several addresses. Reuse of the same deposit address did most of the work.
Friedhelm Victor, “Address Clustering Heuristics for Ethereum”, Financial Cryptography and Data Security 2020

Arkham Intelligence, a blockchain analytics company, opened the Intel Exchange, a marketplace where anyone can post a bounty for the identity behind a wallet, and anyone who supplies it can collect. In its announcement, the company said it believes “deanonymization is destiny in crypto markets.”
CoinDesk, July 2023
Privacy tools don't fix habits

<glossary>Shielded pools</glossary> put many people's deposits into one shared pool, and use cryptography so a withdrawal could have come from any of them. The cryptography can be sound. What gives people away is what they do around it: an unusual amount, a short wait, or money sent straight back to the wallet it came from.

Some newer pool designs are compliance-aware. They let users prove that their withdrawal comes from an approved group of deposits, called an association set, without revealing which deposit is theirs.

Your worst day

Privacy on a public chain doesn't average out. You can be careful for three years and slip once, by funding the wrong wallet or withdrawing too soon. That single link joins everything on both sides of it, backward and forward in time, and the ledger can't be edited.
Your privacy is only as strong as your worst day.
That's why careful people still get linked, and why better defaults matter more than better habits. A setting you have to remember is a setting you'll forget one day.
The technical bit: more patterns analysts use
Token approvals. If one ordinary address gives another permission to move its tokens, the two usually have the same owner. This was the third heuristic in the 2020 study above.

Fees and hours. Researchers profiled Ethereum users by the fees they chose and the hours they were active, and used those patterns to link addresses, including deposits and withdrawals in a popular Ethereum mixer. Béres, Seres, Benczúr and Quintyne-Collins, “Blockchain is Watching You: Profiling and Deanonymizing Ethereum Users”, IEEE DAPPS 2021
What happens next. A withdrawal that goes to the same apps, the same exchange or the same friends as your main wallet links straight back.
Other chains. Bridge an unusual amount to another network a few minutes after it leaves a pool, and the two records line up.
What helps · Part II

An address funded from one you already use is linked from its first transaction. Common amounts and longer waits keep you inside a bigger crowd, while unusual amounts and quick withdrawals shrink it, sometimes to one. A public name links every address it touches.

Here are four bridges people build without noticing.
page-privacy-public-by-default-world-exc: The exchange that has your ID

You probably bought your first ETH on an exchange, after uploading an ID, a selfie and your home address. When you withdrew to your own wallet, the exchange recorded that address next to your name. It has to. Anti-money-laundering rules require exchanges to keep identity records for years, often after you close the account. How long varies by country.

So one company holds the link between your whole cluster and your legal name, and you're trusting everyone who works there, contractors included. Buying a hardware wallet works the same way. The shop knows you own crypto, and where to deliver the box.
page-privacy-public-by-default-world-rec: Criminals paid support staff outside the US to copy customer data from Coinbase's customer support tools: names, home addresses, phone numbers, images of government IDs, balance snapshots and transaction history, for about 69,000 customers.
They demanded $20 million. Coinbase refused and offered a $20 million reward for information on the attackers instead.
Coinbase blog, “Protecting Our Customers: Standing Up to Extortionists”

Point {ensName} at an address, add your social profiles and a photo to its records, and anyone can read all of it. Put the name in your bio and every follower can open your wallet's full history in a couple of clicks.
page-privacy-public-by-default-world-bad: Event badges like <glossary>POAPs</glossary> are tokens sent to your address. Each one says which event, where and when. One badge says you went to a conference. A year of them says which city you live in and which evenings you're out.
page-privacy-public-by-default-world-pay: Everyone you pay learns an address of yours, and most of them already know your name. {friendName} does. So does the café, if you're a regular. Pay the same café every weekday morning and anyone reading the chain can guess your neighborhood.

Badges and payments are ordinary token transfers. A block explorer lists every one for an address, with the date and time.
page-privacy-public-by-default-world-use: What people do with a name and a balance
Usually, nothing dramatic. A landlord checks your savings before renewing your lease. A coworker sees which café you pay on weekday mornings.

Then there are people who want your money. Leaked customer lists feed phishing that knows your name, your address and which wallet you own. Some attackers go further and target people in person. Security researchers call this a wrench attack, because threatening the person who holds the key is easier than breaking the encryption.
page-privacy-public-by-default-world-rec: Security researcher Jameson Lopp keeps a public list of physical attacks on crypto holders. It logged about 70 in 2025, up from about 41 in 2024, the most since the list began in 2014. It only counts attacks that made the news.

page-privacy-public-by-default-fixes-fix: Separate wallets for separate lives
Separate wallets
An hour, then a habit
One wallet for each part of your life, for example income, savings, trading and public. They're kept in different apps or browser profiles, and they never send money to each other.
The links between your addresses. If one of them becomes known, the others stay apart.

Every new address needs ETH for its first transaction fee, and paying it from one of your other addresses links them. Today that takes planning. Frame transactions, scheduled for the Hegotá upgrade, would let another account pay the fee without that link.
<link>See what's planned for privacy on Ethereum</link>.
Read the chain privately
Private reads
A weekend
Instead of asking an RPC service about your balances, your wallet can ask your own <glossary>node</glossary>: a computer running Ethereum software that keeps its own copy of the chain.
Your query history and the link between your addresses. Your own node answers balance questions without telling anyone else.

A machine with a large, fast SSD and some upkeep. Away from home, you need a way to reach it, such as a VPN to your own node. When you send a transaction, your node's peers still see your IP address first, so pair it with hiding your IP.
Home node setups, from a spare computer to plug-and-play hardware, are covered in <link>the guide to running a node</link>.
Hide your IP address
Hide your IP
An hour
Every server your wallet contacts sees your IP address, which reveals roughly where you are. Sending your wallet's traffic through Tor, or through a VPN, hides it from those servers.
Your rough location, and the link between your IP address and your addresses, from RPC services, price services, image hosts and nodes on the network.

It's slower, and some services, including some RPC providers, block Tor. A VPN moves the trust rather than removing it: the VPN service then sees your IP address and every server you contact. Your IP address is only one clue, and everything else they know still counts.
<link>Learn how Tor and VPNs work</link>.
Lock down your wallet's settings
Wallet settings
5 minutes
Many wallets load things in the background every time you open them: token lists, prices and NFT images. Each of those requests carries your IP address.
Turning off automatic NFT images, NFT detection and token detection means fewer services learn your IP address and what you hold.
Fewer pictures, and you may have to add tokens by hand. The wallet's own servers and your <glossary>RPC</glossary> service can still see you.
Many wallets have a privacy setting that stops balance checks for all your accounts in a single request. <link>Compare wallets and their features</link>.
Send trades through a private channel
Private sending
5 minutes
A private transaction channel (sometimes called an MEV-protected RPC) hands your transaction straight to <glossary>block builders</glossary> instead of announcing it to the whole network.

Bots watching the <glossary>mempool</glossary>, the public waiting room for transactions, can't see your trade before it lands, and nodes on the network don't hear about it from your IP address first.

You trust the channel with your transaction and your IP address, and it could delay or drop what you send. Some channels share hints about pending transactions with searchers, the bots that look for profitable trades, so check what a channel shares before you use it.
<link>Learn how MEV works</link>.
Move money through a shielded pool
Shielded pool
An evening, plus fees
A <glossary>shielded pool</glossary> holds many people's funds together. You deposit from one address and later withdraw to a different one.

The link between the address you deposit from and the address you withdraw to. A <glossary>zero-knowledge proof</glossary> shows the pool that a withdrawal matches one of the deposits, without revealing which one.

Fees on the way in and out. A small pool hides you among few people, and exact amounts or quick withdrawals shrink that crowd. Rules on shielded pools differ by country. Some privacy designs rely on cryptography that a future quantum computer might break, which could expose past activity.
Shielded pools are covered on <link>the Ethereum privacy page</link>.
Get paid at stealth addresses
Stealth addresses
An evening
With <glossary>stealth addresses</glossary>, you share one public code, called a stealth meta-address. Each payer sends to a brand-new address that only you can find.
Makes it much harder to add up your income, and stops the people who pay you from seeing who else pays you.
Most wallets don't support stealth addresses yet. If you later move many stealth payments into one address, you link them again.
Stealth-address apps (the standard is ERC-5564) are covered on <link>the Ethereum privacy page</link>.
Break the exchange link
Break the exchange link
Ongoing

An exchange that checked your ID knows every address you withdraw to, and every address that sends to your deposit address. That ties those addresses, and anything linked to them, to your legal name. Exchanges keep this data, can be breached, and share it with authorities when the law requires.
Keeping the addresses you use with an exchange apart from the rest of your activity limits what your exchange account, or a breach of it, can reveal about you.

The exchange still knows what you bought and which addresses you used with it. Exchanges may question, delay or refuse deposits linked to a shielded pool, depending on local rules. Some privacy designs let you prove your funds aren't linked to illicit sources, but whether an exchange accepts that proof varies.
<link>Read about compliance-aware privacy</link>.
Keep your name on a public-only wallet
Public-only name
An hour
Your public self gets its own wallet, holding very little, for your <glossary>ENS name</glossary>, event badges and public donations. It never sends money directly to or from your other wallets.
Your balance, income and payment history, from anyone who looks up your public name.
Two identities to keep apart for as long as you use them. If your name already points at an address you use for savings, that link is already public and can't be removed.
<link>Read about privacy on Ethereum</link>.
Blur your timing and amounts
Blur timing
A habit
Patterns give you away: exact amounts that match, money moving minutes after it arrived, activity at the same hours every day.
Your daily rhythm and time zone, and the matching of deposits to withdrawals by amount and timing. Common amounts and longer waits keep you in a bigger crowd.
It's slower and takes discipline. One rushed transaction can undo it, because the record stays public.
<link>See how analysts match timing and amounts</link>.
Harden your browser
Harden your browser
10 minutes
Websites can read details about your browser and device, and list the wallets you have installed. A browser profile used only for your wallet keeps it away from the rest of your browsing.
Your device fingerprint, the list of wallets you have installed, and the link between your wallet and the accounts you're logged into elsewhere.
Some sites break, or ask you to prove you're human more often. Every profile in the same browser still shares your device's fingerprint.
<link>Learn about private browsers and fingerprinting</link>.
Some designs add association sets: you can also prove that your deposit belongs to a group that excludes funds known to be stolen or illicit, still without revealing which deposit is yours.
A <glossary>light client</glossary> checks that the answers an RPC service gives you are correct, but it doesn't hide what you ask.
page-privacy-public-by-default-fixes-pri: Or turn them all on at once
Today you have to find each of those settings, understand it, set it up and keep it up. One slip, such as paying from the wrong address, and that link stays on the chain.
This is what it would feel like if one switch did all of it.
All {total} fixes on. Everything they knew is blurred out. In real life each one is a separate decision, and it only holds if you keep them all up.
Nothing on. This is what the defaults give you.
page-privacy-public-by-default-fixes-def: That switch should be the default
A private mode you have to go looking for is still opt-in, and most people never change a default. So most people stay exposed.
Ethereum's privacy roadmap points toward private defaults, but much of it is still research and proposals, and most of it isn't in wallets yet. The final chapter shows where it stands.
page-privacy-public-by-default-fixes-inv: Even with every switch on, you're still someone who uses Ethereum. That's fine. The goal is to choose what you reveal, and to whom.
page-privacy-public-by-default-fixes-cro: You're part of someone else's crowd

When you use these tools, you become cover for everyone else who does. That includes people who need privacy far more than you might: someone leaving an abusive partner, a reporter protecting a source, a shop owner who doesn't want competitors reading the books.

Nobody outside the service can check that promise. The service still sees your IP address and your addresses.
The RPC service you picked
Your phone may not be using your node
Unless your phone wallet points at your node and can reach it away from home, it's still asking a default service.
Whichever service your phone asks instead
Your node's peers see your IP address when you send
Reads through your own node stay private. When you send, the peers your node talks to hear about it first, from your IP address.
Nodes on the network
Every payment shows your whole balance
Anyone you pay, and anyone who pays you, can look up your balance and history.
Everyone you transact with
Your pay-me address is public
Everyone who pays you can see who else pays you, and follow what you do with the money.
Everyone who pays you
Your badges put you in a place at a time
Event badges on your main address show which city you were in and when. A few of them sketch your routine.
Anyone
Your trades are visible before they land
Bots watch the <glossary>mempool</glossary>, the public waiting room for transactions, and can place trades around yours. You pay the difference.
Trading bots
Every site can fingerprint you and list your wallets
Your device fingerprint, your installed wallets and the accounts you're logged into, all in one browser.
Every website you visit
Your crypto profile still has your device's fingerprint
A separate profile keeps your logins apart. Your screen, graphics chip and time zone look the same in every profile.
Websites you use for crypto
Your wallet loads things on its own
Token lists, prices and NFT images load in the background, from your IP address, whether or not you look at them.
Price services and NFT image hosts
Your hardware wallet's app still talks to servers
The device keeps your keys offline. Its companion app still asks servers about your balances, like any other wallet.
The companion app's servers
Your login is tied to your address
If you log in with an email or a social account, the wallet provider can link that identity to your address. Smart wallets also send transactions through extra services that see your IP address.
The wallet provider and its services

Helps with: {leaks}
Confirms the rest of your plan worked
Turn off what your wallet loads on its own
Open your wallet's settings and find the privacy or security section.
Turn off NFT images and automatic NFT detection. Hide NFTs you didn't ask for instead of opening them.
Turn off automatic token detection. Many wallets have a privacy setting that stops balance checks for all your accounts in a single request.
Turn off analytics and "help us improve" options.
Learn what your public address reveals
Check which of your addresses or ENS names appear in your bios, on your website or in old posts.
Look one of them up in a block explorer to see what anyone can see: your balance, your history and who you've paid.
Old posts and archives stay public, so an address you've shared is best treated as public from now on.
The fix about keeping your name on a public-only wallet explains how people keep a public name apart from their money.
Give crypto its own browser profile
Create a new browser profile used only for your wallet. Don't log into email or social accounts in it.
Remove the wallet extension from your everyday profile.
Every profile in the same browser shares your device's fingerprint. <link>Learn about browsers that resist fingerprinting</link>.
Look into a private channel for trades
A private transaction channel (sometimes called an MEV-protected RPC) hands your transaction to block builders instead of announcing it to the whole network.
Bots can't see your trade early, and nodes on the network don't hear about it from your IP address.
The trade-off is that the channel sees your transaction and your IP address, and you trust it to pass the transaction on. Some channels share hints with searchers, so check what a channel shares.
Choose who your wallet asks
Find the network or RPC setting in your wallet and check which service it uses today.
If your wallet allows it, use a different service for each account, so no single service sees all of them together.
Treat "no logs" as a promise nobody outside the service can check.
Confirm the change took effect. The section below shows how.
Give each part of your life its own wallet
Decide your contexts, for example public, income, savings and everyday spending.
Make a fresh address for each. Never send money directly between them.
Keep them apart in software too, with one wallet app or profile per context, so no app asks about all of them in the same second.
Plan how each new address will get ETH for its first fee without linking it to the others. The item on funding new addresses explains why this matters.
Learn how a first fee links new addresses
A new address needs ETH for its first transaction fee. If that ETH comes from your main address or straight from an exchange, the two are publicly linked.
Frame transactions, scheduled for the Hegotá upgrade, could let another account, such as a paymaster, pay the fee, so a fresh address doesn't need funding from your main one.
<link>Read about the options on the Ethereum privacy page</link>.
Learn about stealth addresses
Stealth-address apps (the standard is ERC-5564) let you share one stealth meta-address. Each payer sends to a fresh address that only you can find.
Most wallets don't support them yet, so check whether your wallet, and the wallets of people who pay you, can use them.
If you move that money on, merging it all into one address rebuilds the link.
Watch what your wallet sends
Follow "Don't trust, verify" below. It takes about ten minutes.
Do it again after every change you make, to confirm the old traffic really stopped.
Run your own node, and use it
Home node setups range from a spare computer running an execution client and a consensus client to plug-and-play hardware. <link>The guide to running a node</link> walks you through it.
Point every wallet you use at it, including your phone. Away from home, you can reach it through a VPN to your own node.
Your node answers balance questions without telling anyone. When you send, its peers see your IP address first. A private transaction channel hides that, if you trust whoever runs it.
Check that your wallets really use it.
Learn about shielded pools
<link>Read how shielded pools work</link>, including designs that use association sets to show funds aren't linked to known theft.
Common amounts and longer waits make it harder to match a deposit to a withdrawal, because they keep you in a bigger crowd.
Rules on shielded pools differ by country. Check what applies where you live.
Learn how exchanges link your identity
An exchange that checked your ID knows every address you withdraw to and every address that sends to your deposit address.
That data can be breached, and exchanges share it with authorities when the law requires.
Exchanges may question, delay or refuse deposits that came from a shielded pool, depending on local rules. Some privacy designs let you prove your funds aren't linked to illicit sources.
page-privacy-public-by-default-today-ver: Every wallet says it respects your privacy. You can check what it actually sends in about ten minutes, and you don't need to be a developer.
In Chrome or another Chromium-based browser, open the extensions page ({extensionsPage}) and turn on Developer mode.
Find your wallet and click the service worker link next to "Inspect views".
In the developer tools window that opens, choose the Network tab and turn on "Preserve log".
Lock and unlock your wallet, then watch the list fill.
Other browsers have similar developer tools for extensions.
A network monitor for your operating system shows every server an app tries to reach, and many let you block connections you didn't expect.
Most traffic is encrypted, so you'll see where your wallet connects but not what it sends.

On an iPhone, go to Settings, then Privacy & Security, then App Privacy Report, and turn it on. After a day, open your wallet under App Network Activity to see the domains it contacted over the past week.
On Android, a network monitor app can log each app's connections.

page-privacy-public-by-default-default-n: What's being built to make privacy the default, and how far along it is.
page-privacy-public-by-default-default-l: Everything in this lesson describes Ethereum as it works today. Researchers across the ecosystem are working to change the default, so that the private setting is the one you get without asking.
page-privacy-public-by-default-default-s: Some networks made privacy the default years ago. Monero, for example, hides the amount and the receiver of every transaction, and hides the sender among a group of possible senders. That sender hiding is probabilistic: it makes the real sender hard to pick out, not impossible. On Ethereum, privacy is opt-in.

Opting in has a cost. A deposit into a <glossary>shielded pool</glossary> (a shared contract that hides who paid whom) is public, and the address that made it got its gas from somewhere. When only a few people opt in, each of them stands out.
page-privacy-public-by-default-default-c: A shielded pool hides you among everyone else who uses it. Change the size of the crowd, then see what a couple of common habits do to it.
page-privacy-public-by-default-default-r: Ethereum's privacy roadmap groups the work into three areas that match the witnesses from Part I, plus the wallets where you would notice the change.
None of this is finished. Upgrades get proposed, changed, delayed and sometimes dropped.
Hegotá is the upgrade planned after Glamsterdam. Its two headliners, FOCIL and frame transactions, are confirmed. The rest of its contents are still being decided.
Check a balance without telling anyone who you are or what you looked at.
You can already send requests over the <link>Tor network</link> if you set it up yourself. The research aims to make anonymous RPC access and mixnets the default, so no provider sees your IP address.
Private information retrieval (PIR) lets a server answer a question without learning which address you asked about. Teams are testing implementations.
A <glossary>light client</glossary> verifies the data your wallet gets back, so a provider can't quietly give you wrong answers.
Send without the transaction pointing back at you.

Inclusion lists that validators enforce. If a <glossary>block builder</glossary> leaves out a listed transaction, validators can reject the block, which makes private transactions much harder to quietly ignore.
A new transaction type made of steps (frames) that can let another account, such as a paymaster, pay the gas, so a fresh address doesn't need funding from your main one.

Today each sender's transactions must go through in one strict order, so one stuck transaction blocks the rest. Keyed nonces, built on frame transactions, let privacy protocols route many unrelated users through one shared sender address without their transactions blocking each other.
A shielded pool in the protocol (EIP-8182)
A proposed shielded pool built into Ethereum for private ETH and ERC-20 transfers. It was considered for Hegotá but not included, and is still being discussed as an EIP.
Prove a fact about yourself and nothing else.
Show the fact, keep the document

<glossary>Zero-knowledge proofs</glossary> let you prove you're old enough, or a citizen, without showing your ID. Work on zero-knowledge identity (zkID) is lining up with the European Digital Identity (EUDI) wallet, and anonymous credential designs keep separate proofs from being linked back to one profile.
MACI makes it very hard to prove how you voted, so votes are much harder to buy or coerce. clr.fund used MACI for quadratic funding rounds starting in 2020.

It relies on one trust assumption: a coordinator processes the votes and can see how each person voted, so voters have to trust the coordinator to keep that private. The coordinator could also leave some votes out, but it can't change votes or forge the result: zero-knowledge proofs let anyone check the tally.
Researchers are making proofs fast enough for ordinary devices, and working toward post-quantum proofs so that data kept private today isn't exposed later.
Where you would notice the change.

Kohaku is an open-source toolkit and reference wallet for wallet builders, in development and not yet audited. Its roadmap includes private sends and receives in the normal send screen, a new address for each app you connect to, a light client that checks your RPC provider, and fewer IP address leaks.
You probably won't use Kohaku directly. You'd notice it if your own wallet started offering private sends.
